title: EU AI Act's August 2 transparency rules take effect in seven days — high-risk regime delayed
subtitle: Article 50 obligations on disclosing chatbots and labeling deepfakes land on schedule, while the heavier high-risk regime slides more than a year under the Digital Omnibus reset.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The bulk of the EU AI Act's transparency obligations under Article 50 become applicable on August 2. Two requirements do the heavy lifting: any AI system that interacts directly with people must make clear that a person is dealing with a machine unless that is obvious from context, and any deepfake or manipulated audio, image or video must be disclosed as artificially generated. The rules apply to any provider or deployer whose system reaches EU users, not only to companies headquartered in the bloc — and enforcement powers, including administrative fines, sit with national market surveillance authorities from August 2 onward.

The Digital Omnibus on AI, given final Council approval on June 29, split the AI Act calendar into two speeds. Transparency lands on the original schedule. The heavier high-risk regime — the classification, documentation, conformity assessment and human oversight requirements that most industry pushback has focused on — slides more than a year into the future. One narrow carve-out on the transparency side: Article 50(2), which requires machine-readable marking of synthetic audio, image, video or text output, only applies from December 2 for systems already on the market before August 2, giving providers a four-month transitional window on watermarking and content-labeling infrastructure.

The practical scope is wider than most companies realize. Article 50 applies to consumer chatbots, customer-service assistants, voice agents, image generators, video-editing tools and any product feature that could be mistaken for human-generated content. It applies whether the underlying model is proprietary or open-weight. And it applies to deployers as well as providers — a company that integrates a third-party model into its own product still owes the disclosure to its users. The European Commission's AI Office published a template disclosure format in mid-July, but companies are free to design their own as long as the notice is clear, distinguishable, and delivered at the first meaningful interaction.

For learners: if you are building anything users interact with in Europe, the operational deadline is real, and the fix is small enough that there is no reason to miss it. Add a first-interaction disclosure for chatbots and voice agents ('you're chatting with an AI'). Add a visible label to AI-generated or AI-edited media outputs. Both are one-line UI changes, not architectural ones, and both are the kind of item that turns into a regulator letter if you skip them. The high-risk regime is the fight you can afford to prepare for over the next year; the transparency layer is the one that becomes law next Sunday.
